newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: PLO says it may take settlement issue to U.N. again.
newsitem.headline: PLO says it may take settlement issue to U.N. again.

text.p: The Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) said on Friday it would turn again to the United Nations if Israel continued building a housing project in East Jerusalem.

PLO U.N. observer Nasser al-Kidwa spoke to reporters after the fourth U.N. debate since early March on Israel's decision to proceed with the construction of 6,500 homes for Jews at a site between Jerusalem and Bethlehem called Har Homa in Hebrew and Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic.

"The Israeli government cannot go on with the peace process on one hand and the settlement activities on the other hand. They have to make up their mind," he said. "Accordingly we say, if the Israeli government decides to choose the continuation of the settlement activities, then we will have no option but to continue with our political confrontation at all levels, including at the United Nations -- at the Security Council and at the emergency special session as well."

The General Assembly, at a rare emergency special session that can be resumed, voted on Friday 134-3, with 11 abstentions, to demand an immediate halt to the Israeli building project. It also called for the cessation of all forms of assistance and support for "illegal Israeli activities" in the occupied territories.

Last month two Security Council debates on the issue ended with vetoes by the United States and a non-emergency assembly session adopted a resolution 130-2, with two abstentions, calling on Israel to abandon the construction. There is no veto in the assembly, whose decisions are not binding.

"The whole international community is awaiting Israel's response," al-Kidwa said, noting the latest resolution asked Secretary-General Kofi Annan to report on its implementation within two months. "We might react if we see ... clear signals that the Israeli government chooses to defy international law and the international community one more time."
American U.N. envoy Bill Richardson, who voted against the resolution, told reporters it "contained very negative elements," even though it had been "watered down."

"I think the abstentions by several key European countries show their concern that this is an issue that does not belong in the General Assembly," he added, reiterating the U.S. view that differences between Israel and the Palestinians should be resolved through direct negotiations.

Israeli U.N. envoy David Peleg issued a statement saying there was "no procedural or substantive justification" for convening an emergency session of the assembly "concerning the construction of a residential neighbourhood in Jerusalem. This, while the international agenda is laden with genuine problems which require urgent attention."

Israel "categorically rejects the one-sided resolution ... which stands in contradiction to the peace process and its principles," he said. "Israel believes that all outstanding issues will be resolved only through direct negotiations between the parties concerned, within the framework of the peace process."
